# proxy-cover

**What a garment does to the skin under it**, as numbers: the half of
[human-proxy](/human-proxy/)'s `coverBody` that needs no engine, so an
exporter (or another engine) hides the skin exactly as the builder does.

- Skin a garment LISTS (`delete`) is tucked in along its normal by `tuck`
  metres, and its triangles are dropped (glasses excepted: they list the lids
  under the lenses, which they do not cover).
- Skin a garment that WRAPS the body (`BODY_WRAPPING_SLOTS`) covers without
  listing it, found by geometry from the garment's drawn positions, is tucked
  just far enough to sit under it: 4 mm, more where it is loose, never more
  than 10 mm.
- Every tuck FADES IN over `fade` metres from the edge of the covered skin,
  so a cuff or a neckline shows no dip.

```javascript
import { coverSkin } from 'tosijs-3d/proxy-cover'
const { positions, deleted } = coverSkin(untucked, normals, triangles, vertices, wearing, { drawn })
```

`coverDepths` is the rule alone (how deep each vertex goes, before the
fade), for anything that measures against it.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/proxy-cover/

---

# skinned-glb

**A skinned, morphing mesh out as a GLB.** `writeSkinnedGlb` writes one
skeleton, any number of meshes skinned to it (four influences a vertex), each
with morph targets named in `extras.targetNames`, and plain glTF
metallic-roughness materials with their images embedded. Pure: no Babylon,
no DOM, synchronous, bytes out. It is `writeGarmentGlb`'s sibling for rigged
bodies, which that writer does not do (no skin, no morphs).

Part of the [character core](/character-core/): import it as
`tosijs-3d/skinned-glb`. Written for Dramatis's character exporter (GLB and
VRM), and checked against the Khronos validator and Babylon's own loader.

```javascript
import { writeSkinnedGlb } from 'tosijs-3d/skinned-glb'
const bytes = writeSkinnedGlb({ asset, joints, skinName, skeletonRoot, inverseBindMatrices, meshes, materials, images })
```

What it guarantees, so the Khronos validator is clean:

- joints are nodes `0..n-1`, in the order given, each parent before its
  children; every mesh is its own top-level node with no transform;
- `POSITION` accessors (and every morph target's) carry `min` and `max`;
- normals are unit length (a zero normal becomes +Y); weights are
  renormalised in float32 so each vertex's sum is 1, and a joint never
  appears twice in one vertex's non-zero slots;
- indices are `UNSIGNED_SHORT` below 65,535 vertices, `UNSIGNED_INT` above;
- morph targets are sparse accessors over the vertices they move (a target
  that moves nothing is the caller's to leave out; one here throws);
- `KHR_materials_sheen` is listed in `extensionsUsed` only when a material
  has sheen; nothing is ever required.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/skinned-glb/

---

# rigged-body-glb

**Any rigged body out as a skinned GLB that plays UAL's clips by name.** A
body the rig tool made (an AI mesh, an artist's mesh, a scan), a file's own
skin, or MakeHuman's: `riggedBodyGlb(body)` writes it in the same profile as
Dramatis's character export, so three.js, Unity, Godot and Blender open it
and a UAL clip binds to its bones with no retargeting. Pure: no engine, bytes
out. `tosijs-3d/rigged-body-glb`.

```javascript
import { glbRigTriangles } from 'tosijs-3d/glb-rig'
import { bodyFromMarkers } from 'tosijs-3d/rigged-body'
import { riggedBodyGlb } from 'tosijs-3d/rigged-body-glb'

const body = bodyFromMarkers(glbRigTriangles(bytes), { markers })
const glb = riggedBodyGlb(body, { restPose: 't-pose', naming: 'ue' })
```

What the file is (Dramatis's `export-format`, version 1):

- **The skeleton**: one skin, `skeleton`, over the profile's 65 joints in its
  order (UE mannequin names as UAL spells them: `Head`, `_leaf` tips), or
  Mixamo's names with `naming: 'mixamo'` (`root` keeps its name). Every
  joint's rest ROTATION is UAL's own frame (`ual-rest`), only its position
  is the body's: that is what makes UAL's rotation keys mean the same thing
  on it. A joint the body lacks is placed along UAL's bone, scaled to the
  body; one the profile lacks (a tail) follows after the 65, in its
  parent's frame.
- **The rest pose**: a T-pose by default (arms straight out, palms down, as
  UAL stands; VRM needs one), reached by turning each limb bone onto UAL's
  and skinning the mesh there once; the feet are turned back so they stay
  flat. `restPose: 'source'` keeps the body as it was rigged, UAL's frames
  turned along its bones.
- **Root at the feet**: the soles at y = 0 and the pelvis over the origin,
  metres, Y up, facing +Z. `height` scales the body to a height in metres
  first (a mesh generator's 1.9 units, say, made a real 1.7 m).
- **Meshes**: `body`, one primitive per material, and `eyes` (both eyeballs,
  skinned wholly to `Head`, which the profile prefers to parenting a mesh
  under a joint; with `eyeTexture`, eye-art's picture laid on each by
  `gltfEyeUvs`, else plain white). The file's own materials go out as glTF PBR with their
  pictures embedded, when the body's surfaces carry them as data (a body
  read by `glb-rig`); otherwise a plain grey.
- **Springs**, when given the rig `recipe`: a bone spring (a tail) swings
  from its root down, a strand is baked into joints under its anchor and a
  tube skinned to them, colliders (`auto`: head, chest, clavicles, sized to
  the body) go on their bones. They are written as `VRMC_springBone`, which
  three-vrm, UniVRM and Godot's VRM importer read with no setup, and as
  `TOSIJS_spring_chains`, our own settings exactly (see
  [spring-vrm](/spring-vrm/) for how the two models differ).
- **Garments**, with `garments`: proxies bound to this body (`garmentProxy`
  from a garment file: the tailor's cuts and draped cloth, or a garment
  from Blender), each a mesh named for its slot, skinned with weights from
  the body's own, as the builder draws them (armour lifted 5 mm), with its
  material as data (its pictures, and its saved look's glTF factors where
  it has a plain reading). A recoloured cloth's picture is written
  recoloured when you pass `bake: bakeClothLook` ([cloth-bake](/cloth-bake/),
  PNG or JPEG in, PNG out), so the file shows what the builder does in any
  engine; without it the pictures go as they came, and the writer carries no
  image decoder. The skin they cover is tucked under them, as the
  builder does, and skin a garment lists in its `delete` (as MakeHuman's
  clothes do) is dropped; `cover: false` leaves the skin alone.
- **Clips**, with `clips`: animations read from any skinned GLB
  ([[glb-clips]]: UAL's, Mixamo's, Meshy's) retargeted onto this skeleton
  and written as glTF animations, 30 keys a second by default (rotations,
  and the hips' travel), each with its own `extras` (its licence).
- **A held item**, with `held`: a joint named `weapon_r` (or `held.name`)
  under the hand, where a grip (see [[hold-grip]]) puts the item's grip
  point, turned as the grip says, in the hand's socket frame
  ([[hand-socket]]): the same place the character builder shows it. Unity
  and Unreal attach their own items to a named bone like this one. With
  `held.item` (a mesh in its own frame, as `glbRigTriangles(bytes, { pick })`
  reads one out of a library file) the item goes in too, as a mesh `held`
  skinned wholly to that joint, scaled by the grip's `scale`, its grip
  point (`held.gripPoint`, else the middle of its lowest third) on the
  joint, its own materials and pictures, and `held.extras` (its licence) on
  the mesh, as its file has it.
- **`asset.extras`** is passed through as given (Dramatis's licence block
  goes there), with `generator` and `copyright`.

Weights are the body's own, four per vertex, renormalised.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/rigged-body-glb/

---

# spring-vrm

**Our spring chains as glTF: `VRMC_springBone`, plus our own record of
them.** A rigged body's springs (a tail, a ponytail, a strand hung from a
bone) go out in the standard every VRM loader reads (three-vrm's
`VRMSpringBoneLoaderPlugin`, UniVRM, Godot's VRM importer), so they swing
in those engines with no setup. Beside it goes `TOSIJS_spring_chains`, which
holds the springs exactly as our model has them, so a file read back here
swings as it did when it was made. `riggedBodyGlb` writes both (pass it the
rig recipe); this module is the conversion and the schema, pure.

## Where the two models differ

Our chain (`spring-chain`) is Verlet at a fixed 120 Hz: velocity kept at
`1 - damping` per second, gravity an acceleration, and each point PULLED
toward its rest place by a fraction that grows with `stiffness`, so the
restoring force grows with how far it is out. VRM's (three-vrm's
`VRMSpringBoneJoint.update`, once a frame) adds the last frame's movement
times `1 - dragForce`, then `stiffness × dt` metres along the bone's rest
axis and `gravityPower × dt` metres along `gravityDir`, then keeps the
length. So:

- **Drag** is per FRAME there, per second here: `dragForce = 1 - (1 -
  damping)^(1/60)`, exact at 60 frames a second. VRM's motion depends on the
  frame rate (the specification says so); ours does not.
- **Gravity** adds displacement times `dt` there, so it acts like an
  acceleration of `gravityPower / dt`: `gravityPower = gravity / 60`, exact
  at 60 frames a second.
- **Stiffness** cannot be matched exactly: VRM pushes the tip back with the
  same force however far it is out, ours with a force in proportion. We
  match how far a LEVEL segment droops under gravity: ours settles where the
  pull balances gravity, VRM's where `tan θ = gravityPower / stiffness`.
  Swings away from that settle differently (VRM's springs come back at a
  constant speed and do not ring as ours do).
- **Measured on the weasel's tail** (five joints, our default settings, the
  file read by three-vrm with nothing set up by hand): standing, the tip
  settles 26 cm lower in three-vrm and 43 cm lower in ours; run sideways at
  3 m/s for half a second and stopped, it swings about as far and as long in
  both (still ±0.3 m two seconds later, which is what our defaults are).
  VRM bends each joint from its parent's current direction, ours from the
  anchor's, so a long chain droops less there.
- **Colliders** are spheres in both, on a joint, with an offset in the
  joint's own frame; VRM gives each spring the collider GROUPS it meets.
  Our chain radius is VRM's `hitRadius`.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/spring-vrm/

---

# body export

**A rigged body out as a GLB, from a panel.** The rows the rig tool and the
character builder put in their **Export** section: which joint names, which
rest pose, how tall, and a button that writes the body shown with
[rigged-body-glb](/rigged-body-glb/) (its springs too, from the rig recipe)
and downloads it. The file plays UAL's clips by name in three.js, Unity,
Godot and Blender; a tail or a strand swings in any VRM loader. With
**animation** set to the clip playing, that clip goes in too, retargeted onto
the skeleton as written (from UAL's file, a GLB's animations or a BVH
capture: `clip` on the target says which).

The body on screen was read through Babylon, so its materials are Babylon's.
For the file, the model it came from is read again from its bytes
([glb-rig](/glb-rig/)), and its materials go out as glTF with their
pictures. A model that is not a GLB (an OBJ) goes out in plain grey.

```javascript
import { exportBodyRows } from 'tosijs-3d/body-export'
panel.push(...exportBodyRows(() => ({ body, recipe, source: { url } }), say))
```

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/body-export/

---

# glb-chunks

**A GLB's two chunks, read and written, and its accessors read back.** The
GLB container module new readers and writers use (`skinned-glb`, and
Dramatis's VRM writer, hair reader and gates), so a check reads exports with
the reader the shipped code uses. Pure: no DOM, no engine, synchronous.
`tosijs-3d/glb-chunks`.

Reading, `readGlb`:

- under 12 bytes, a bad magic or a version other than 2 throws "not a GLB";
- a file shorter than its header's length, or a chunk running past it, throws
  "truncated GLB" (a short read, not a corrupt file);
- the first JSON chunk wins, and so does the first BIN chunk;
- the binary chunk is optional (`bin: null`); no JSON chunk throws.

Writing, `writeGlb`: the JSON padded with spaces and the binary chunk with
zeros, to 4 bytes; a null or empty binary chunk is left out, as the spec
allows a GLB with no buffer.

Accessors, `accessorBytes` / `accessorValues` / `readVec3`: tightly packed,
strided views de-interleaved, sparse accessors applied (one with no
`bufferView` starts from zeros, as glTF says), every read bounds-checked
against its buffer view.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/glb-chunks/

---

# glb-rig

**A mesh file's triangles for rigging, read with no engine.** The same
`BodyTriangles` that `loadRigTriangles` (rig-build) gives from a Babylon
scene, read straight from a GLB's bytes: in Bun or Node, in a worker, in a
test, or in a headless export. Hand the result to `bodyFromMarkers` with a
character file's markers and you have its `RiggedBody` with no scene at all.

```javascript
import { glbRigTriangles } from 'tosijs-3d/glb-rig'
import { bodyFromMarkers } from 'tosijs-3d/rigged-body'

const bytes = new Uint8Array(await (await fetch(url)).arrayBuffer())
const tris = glbRigTriangles(bytes)
const body = bodyFromMarkers(tris, { markers, source: url })
```

What it gives, and how it agrees with the Babylon path (a test loads the
same files both ways and compares them):

- **The file's own frame**, right-handed, every node's transform applied.
  A skinned mesh is taken skinned AT REST (its joints' rest transforms times
  their inverse bind matrices), its own node's transform ignored, as glTF
  says and Babylon's loader does: a file in centimetres sized by its
  armature comes out in metres.
- **`pick`** takes one node of a library file and its children, its own
  translation dropped (so the character stands at the origin), as
  `loadRigTriangles` does. A name that is not there throws.
- **Surfaces**: one run of triangles per material, named as Babylon names
  them (the material's name, `material<i>` when it has none, made unique),
  runs that follow one another with the same material joined. Each carries
  its glTF material as data (`GltfSurfaceMaterial`): the PBR factors, alpha
  mode, two-sidedness, and each texture's IMAGE BYTES and MIME type (a
  `data:` URI decoded; an external `uri` kept as it is, unread).
- **Eyes**: meshes named as eyes (`isEyeName`) are kept out of the body and
  handed back as `eyes`, one per side, as `splitEyes` does.
- **Uvs and colours** when any mesh has them (others filled with 0 and white,
  as the Babylon path fills them); colours as RGBA floats.

Only triangle lists are read (mode 4, the default); other primitives (lines,
points, strips) are skipped. Compressed geometry (Draco, meshopt) is not
read: it throws, naming the extension.

The rig from it is DETERMINISTIC: the same bytes and the same markers give
the same weights, so a saved character exports the same every time.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/glb-rig/

---

# skin paint

**The skin's colour, per vertex, with no engine**: the lips and stubble the
character builder paints over a body, as numbers an exporter writes out. The
skin's material carries one colour (`skinAlbedo`, from
[skin-tone](/skin-tone/)'s dials); these are RATIOS over it, one per skin
vertex, so the drawn colour is material × vertex colour. glTF does exactly
that with a vertex colour (`COLOR_0` multiplies the base colour), so a
character written by [skinned-glb](/skinned-glb/) with them looks the same
in any engine that reads glTF, with no texture to bake.

```javascript
import { lipTint, stubbleMask, stubbleTint } from 'tosijs-3d/skin-paint'
import { skinAlbedo } from 'tosijs-3d/skin-tone'
const colours = lipTint(skin, lips, tone, redness)              // RGBA per skin vertex
const mask = stubbleMask({ skin: body, normals, vertices: skin.vertices, positions, lips, beard })
stubbleTint(colours, mask, 0.6, skinAlbedo(tone, redness), hairRgb)
```

- `lipTint`: toward the lips' own albedo where the pack's `lips` region
  says so, feathered at its edge.
- `stubbleMask`: where stubble grows, measured from a full beard fitted to
  this body (and a moustache, which the full beard lacks): below the cheeks,
  not on the lips, and down the front and sides of the neck, fading.
- `stubbleTint`: the skin there toward a darkened, slightly cool hair
  colour (short hairs read as a shadow), by an amount (0 clean-shaven).
- `skinSurface`: the skin as an exporter writes it, a glTF material in the
  skin's albedo and the colours with their alpha set to 1 (the builder keeps
  the skin's thinness there for its back-light, which glTF would read as
  opacity). A `RiggedBody`'s `surfaces` and `colors` take them, and
  `riggedBodyGlb` writes the skin as the builder shows it.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/skin-paint/

---

# cloth bake

**A recoloured garment as a picture**, with no engine: what
[cloth-shading](/cloth-shading/)'s recolour does in a shader, done to the
texture's pixels, so an export carries the colour the character builder
shows in a plain glTF base-colour texture any engine draws.

The recolour reads the texture as grey (its shading: folds, stitching, a
weave), tints it, and blends by `amount` (0 keeps the texture's own colours,
1 is the colour wholly). The tint is divided by the texture's MEAN brightness
so a dark texture tinted keeps the colour's value rather than going darker
still; `textureMean` measures it exactly as the shader's material does.

```javascript
import { pngDecode, pngEncode } from 'tosijs-3d/png'
import { recolourCloth, clothSheenColour } from 'tosijs-3d/cloth-bake'
const shirt = pngDecode(bytes)
const red = recolourCloth(shirt, '#7a2e2e', 0.8)
const png = pngEncode(red.data, red.width, red.height)
const sheen = clothSheenColour('#7a2e2e')   // KHR_materials_sheen's colour, linear
```

`bakeClothLook(picture, look)` is the whole step for a garment: its picture
(PNG or JPEG bytes, [jpeg](/jpeg/)) and the cloth look it is worn with give
the recoloured picture as a PNG, or null when the look leaves the picture as
it is. `riggedBodyGlb` does this to every garment it writes when it is passed as
`bake`.

HAIR TOO: `recolourHair(image, base, highlight)` is
[hair-shading](/hair-shading/) on pixels, for a hairstyle's texture: each
strand's brightness over the texture's mean (`hairMean`, only where there is
hair) times the base colour, the brightest strands leaning to the highlight.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/cloth-bake/

---

# jpeg

**A JPEG read with no engine**: the picture as RGBA bytes, the same
`RgbaImage` that `pngDecode` gives, so a garment's JPEG texture
can be recoloured ([cloth-bake](/cloth-bake/)) and written into an export on
a server, in a worker or in another engine's page.

```javascript
import { jpegDecode, decodeImage } from 'tosijs-3d/jpeg'
const shirt = jpegDecode(bytes) // { width, height, data }
const any = decodeImage(bytes) // a PNG or a JPEG, by its first bytes
```

It reads baseline and progressive JPEGs, grey or colour (YCbCr, or RGB when
the file says so), with any chroma subsampling and restart markers: every
JPEG among MakeHuman's garment textures. Chroma is upsampled with the
triangle filter libjpeg uses, so colours agree with a browser's to a level
or two. Arithmetic coding, 12-bit samples, lossless JPEG and CMYK throw,
naming what they found.

Pure: no DOM, no canvas.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/jpeg/

---

# eye art

**Eyes from a picture**: Tonio Loewald's eye art (CC0, `basic` and `anime`,
served from the asset CDN as 256 × 256 PNGs and the SVGs they are drawn
from), its iris recoloured to any eye colour, in plain code. No engine and no
canvas, so an exporter bakes the same eyes the builder shows:

```javascript
import { eyePngUrl, recolourEyePng, gltfEyeUvs } from 'tosijs-3d/eye-art'
const art = new Uint8Array(await (await fetch(eyePngUrl('basic'))).arrayBuffer())
const png = recolourEyePng(art, '#3f6fa0')  // the eye texture, as a PNG
const uvs = gltfEyeUvs(eyePositions)       // both eyeballs onto that one picture
```

**Recolouring.** The art paints its iris in browns. Inside the iris disc,
every pixel that is a brown takes the new colour at its own lightness, so the
fibres, the darkening toward the rim and the rim itself survive; the art's
middle brown (`#8c6239`) becomes the colour exactly. Greys (the pupil, the
glints) and everything outside the disc are left alone.

**The picture's layout** (`ONE_EYE_LAYOUT`): one eye, the iris centred, 48 px
of radius in 256. `gltfEyeUvs` maps an eyes part holding both eyeballs onto
it in glTF's convention (right-handed, v down from the top), both eyes the
same way round so a glint sits on the same side of each. In Babylon,
[human-face](/human-face/)'s `eyeTexture({ style })` paints the same art.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/eye-art/

---

# hair place

**Hair placed on a body, with no engine**: the geometry half of
[human-hair](/human-hair/). Quaternius' CC0 hairstyles are each modelled in
place on one of Quaternius' heads, so a piece is carried from THAT head to a
body's head: `headScalp` measures the body's head and warps the library
head's skin onto it ([hair-fit](/hair-fit/)), and `placeHair` takes a piece
through the warp, keeps each vertex's height above the skin, lays a
moustache's lower edge on the top of this upper lip, applies any hand
`nudge`, and pushes anything left inside the skin back out.

```javascript
import { readHairLibrary, referenceHeads, closestHead, headScalp, placeHair, hairFitFor } from 'tosijs-3d/hair-place'
const pieces = readHairLibrary(glbBytes)            // the library, read from its GLB
const heads = referenceHeads(pieces)                // the heads it was modelled on
const scalp = headScalp(pack.manifest, positions, triangles, { lips })
const piece = pieces.find((p) => p.name === 'Hair_Buzzed')
const head = closestHead(piece.parts, heads)
const placed = piece.parts.map((part) => placeHair(scalp, part, { head, on: hairFitFor(piece.name, piece.category) }))
```

[human-hair](/human-hair/) loads the same library into Babylon and places
it with these functions, so an exporter (or another engine) puts every piece
exactly where the character builder does.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/hair-place/

---

# mesh sdf

**Is this point inside that mesh, and by how much?** `meshSdf(positions,
triangles)` builds a signed distance to a triangle mesh: `nearest(x, y, z)`
is negative inside. [fit-extremes](/fit-extremes/) uses it to find a garment
inside a body.

```javascript
import { meshSdf } from 'tosijs-3d/mesh-sdf'
const sdf = meshSdf(body.positions, body.triangles)
sdf.nearest(0, 1.2, 0.05).distance   // metres, negative inside the body
```

A point's distance is to the nearest point on the mesh (found through a
uniform grid of triangles); its sign comes from the angle-weighted
pseudo-normal of the feature it is nearest (face, edge or vertex), which
is exact for a closed, consistently wound mesh (Baerentzen and Aanaes,
"Signed distance computation using the angle weighted pseudonormal", 2005).
A body mesh is not quite closed (MakeHuman's has open boundaries at the
eyes and mouth), and the pseudo-normal is only trustworthy near the
surface, so for a point further than `voteBeyond` from it the sign is also
put to a vote of three rays (crossing parity, through the same grid), and
the vote wins. That is the robust part: near the skin, where penetration is
measured in millimetres, the pseudo-normal; deep inside, where a hole in
the mesh could fool it, parity.

Pure: positions xyz (metres), triangles in threes, counter-clockwise
outward (the human pack's winding).

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/mesh-sdf/

---

# fit extremes

**Every garment and hairstyle, on the bodies at the sliders' corners.** A
character is judged on its worst screenshot, and the worst ones are at the
extremes: the heaviest, most muscular, tallest, oldest bodies, the ancestry
corners, the local shapes pushed all the way. This sweep morphs each of those
bodies, fits everything that can be worn as the character builder fits it,
and measures:

- **penetration**: garment and hair vertices inside the body, raw (inside
  the bare skin) and VISIBLE (deeper than the builder tucks the skin there,
  so skin would show through the cloth);
- **bone sanity**: the skeleton `humanRig` fits each body, against the
  default body's (scale after height, left against right, chain order,
  joints inside the skin);
- and draws a **contact sheet** of the worst cases, headless (a software
  rasteriser into a PNG).

It runs with no engine and no DOM:

```sh
bun run extremes                 # the full sweep: 133 bodies, about half an hour
bun run extremes --quick         # the default body and 32 macro corners
bun run extremes --only casual   # only the garments whose names match
bun run extremes --sheet         # also draw the contact sheet
```

It reads MakeHuman's pack and Quaternius' hair library from `../static-assets`
when that is checked out (else from the CDN), and writes
`reviews/extremes/extremes.md` (each item's verdict: holds, fails at the
extremes, or broken at the default), `extremes.json` and the sheet.

The same parts are a library (`tosijs-3d/fit-extremes`): `sweepCorners`
lists the bodies, `runSweep({ pack, corners, proxies, hair })` measures
them, `summarise` and `renderMarkdown` report, `contactSheet` draws.
`penetration` and `checkBones` work on any body, with
[mesh-sdf](/mesh-sdf/) as the inside test.

**The bodies** (`sweepCorners`, 133): the default; every corner of the six
macros that blend as corners (gender, age from 25 to 90, muscle, weight,
height, proportions: 64), because they interact and only the full product
finds the bad combinations; each pure ancestry on eight gender, weight and
muscle corners (24); and each local shape (bust size and firmness, waist,
chest depth, pecs) at each end on four bases, plus the four with all of them
out at once (44). Children are not swept.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/fit-extremes/

---

# retarget

**One humanoid's animation on another humanoid's body.** The Universal
Animation Library's clips are authored on the UE mannequin; a Mixamo
character, a Kenney chibi or a model of your own has different bone names,
a different number of bones, a different rest pose and different
proportions. This makes the clips play anyway.

## Demo

```js
import { b3d, b3dLight, assetUrl, readSkeleton, retargetClip, select3d } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { tosi } from 'tosijs'

const { rt } = tosi({ rt: { clip: 'Walk_Loop' } })
const clips = ['Idle_Loop', 'Walk_Loop', 'Jog_Fwd_Loop', 'Sprint_Loop', 'Dance_Loop', 'Crouch_Fwd_Loop', 'Swim_Fwd_Loop', 'Pistol_Idle_Loop']

preview.append(
  b3d(
    {
      clearColor: '#2a3340',
      panelTitle: 'Retarget',
      scenePanel: () => [select3d({ label: 'clip', value: rt.clip, options: clips })],
      async sceneCreated(el, BABYLON) {
        const scene = el.scene
        const cam = new BABYLON.ArcRotateCamera('c', Math.PI / 2, 1.35, 7, new BABYLON.Vector3(0, 0.8, 0), scene)
        cam.attachControl(el.querySelector('canvas'), true)
        el.setActiveCamera(cam)
        const ground = BABYLON.MeshBuilder.CreateGround('g', { width: 12, height: 6 }, scene)
        ground.position.y = -0.01

        const load = async (url) => {
          const c = await BABYLON.LoadAssetContainerAsync(url, scene)
          c.addAllToScene()
          for (const g of c.animationGroups) g.stop()
          return c
        }
        const rootOf = (c) => c.meshes.find((m) => m.name === '__root__')
        // One character out of a library file: hide the rest, find its skin.
        const pick = (c, name) => {
          const top = c.transformNodes.find((n) => n.name === name) || c.meshes.find((n) => n.name === name)
          for (const m of c.meshes) if (m.name !== '__root__' && top && !m.isDescendantOf(top) && m !== top) m.setEnabled(false)
          if (top) top.position.set(0, 0, 0)
          return c.skeletons.find((s) => s.bones.some((b) => { const t = b.getTransformNode(); return t && top && t.isDescendantOf(top) }))
        }

        const ual = await load(assetUrl('quaternius/UAL1_core.glb', 3))
        const source = readSkeleton(ual.skeletons[0], rootOf(ual))
        const bodies = [{ root: rootOf(ual), skeleton: null, x: 2.4 }]
        const hero = await load(assetUrl('quaternius/libraries/characters-superhero-male.glb'))
        bodies.push({ root: rootOf(hero), skeleton: pick(hero, 'Superhero_Male_FullBody'), x: 0.8 })
        const omni = await load('/omnidude.glb')
        bodies.push({ root: rootOf(omni), skeleton: omni.skeletons[0], x: -0.8 })
        const mini = await load(assetUrl('kenney/libraries/mini-characters.glb'))
        const miniSkin = pick(mini, 'character-female-a')
        rootOf(mini).scaling.scaleInPlace(3)
        bodies.push({ root: rootOf(mini), skeleton: miniSkin, x: -2.4, armSpaceDeg: 55 })

        for (const b of bodies) {
          b.root.position.x = b.x
          if (b.skeleton) b.read = readSkeleton(b.skeleton, b.root)
        }
        // Retarget each clip once per body, the first time it is asked for.
        const made = new Map()
        let playing = []
        const play = (name) => {
          for (const g of playing) g.stop()
          const clip = ual.animationGroups.find((g) => g.name === name)
          if (!clip) return
          playing = bodies.map((b, i) => {
            if (!b.read) return clip
            const key = name + i
            if (!made.has(key)) made.set(key, retargetClip(clip, source, b.read, { scene, armSpaceDeg: b.armSpaceDeg }))
            return made.get(key)
          })
          for (const g of playing) g.start(true)
        }
        play(rt.clip.value)
        rt.clip.observe(() => play(rt.clip.value))
      },
    },
    b3dLight({ intensity: 0.9 })
  )
)
```

One clip, four bodies. On the right, UAL's own mannequin plays the original;
then the same clip retargeted onto a Quaternius superhero (the same 65 bones,
other proportions), omnidude (Mixamo's bones, 0.88 m tall) and a Kenney
chibi (seven bones: one for each whole leg, arm and the torso; shown three
times its size). Pick a clip in the panel.

A chibi's arms are long for its height: hanging where the clip's hang, its
hands would go through the floor. `armSpaceDeg` (Mixamo's "Character
Arm-Space") turns the upper arms out from the body, and the chibi takes 55°.

## How it works

1. **Roles.** `humanoidRoles(bones)` says which bone is the hips, the chest,
   the left forearm, … from the names and the hierarchy, across the common
   spellings (UE `upperarm_l`, Mixamo `mixamorig:LeftArm`, Kenney `arm-left`,
   Blender `forearm.L`), and each finger's three joints (`index_01_l`,
   `LeftHandIndex1`, `thumb.01.L`). Twist, IK and end bones are left alone.
2. **Rotations, not positions.** `retargeter(source, target).pose` gives each target bone the
   world-space rotation its source bone made since ITS rest, so bone
   lengths are the target's own: a long-legged clip on a short-legged body
   bends the same joints by the same angles.
3. **Rest poses that disagree.** A clip authored on an A-pose rig, played on
   a T-pose one, must still put the arms where the clip shows them, not 45°
   higher. Each target bone is first lined up with its source bone's rest
   direction (toward the next joint down the limb; a hand toward a finger
   both rigs have), so poses come across as the clip shows them, whatever
   rest pose either rig was bound in.
4. **The hips move in proportion.** Their translation is scaled by the ratio
   of hip heights, so a short character's stride is shorter, not stretched.
5. **Feet on the ground stay there.** The same angles on a leg whose thigh
   and shin are proportioned differently put the foot somewhere else: a
   crouch on a long-thighed body lifts one foot off the floor. So each foot
   near the ground goes as high as the source's went (its travel scaled as
   the hips' is; the ball, when the source is on its toes), keeping the
   clip's place across the floor, and the thigh and shin bend to reach it,
   the knee the way the clip bends it (toward the leg's front when the leg
   is nearly straight). A foot in the air keeps the copied angles.
   `footIk: false` turns it off.

Babylon-free and deterministic (plain `{x, y, z, w}` quaternions), like
`fly-by-wire`: the Babylon side (`retarget-babylon`) reads the skeletons and
writes the result.

A mesh with no skeleton at all can be rigged for these clips too: the
[rig tool](/rig-tool/) fits a skeleton from eight markers dragged over the
mesh, as Mixamo's auto-rigger does, and binds the mesh to it
([auto-rig](/rig-build/) is the code underneath).

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/retarget/

---

# glb clips

**A GLB's animations, read and retargeted with no engine.** Any skinned GLB
carries its clips (Mixamo's, Meshy's, UAL's) as keyframes on its skeleton.
`readGlbClips` reads them, and the skeleton they were made on, from the bytes;
`bakeClip` samples one through [[retarget]] onto another skeleton as
keyframes; `riggedBodyGlb`'s `clips` writes them into an exported body, so a
character leaves with its walk cycle.

```javascript
import { readGlbClips, bakeClip } from 'tosijs-3d/glb-clips'
import { riggedBodyGlb } from 'tosijs-3d/rigged-body-glb'

const ual = readGlbClips(new Uint8Array(await (await fetch(ualUrl)).arrayBuffer()))
ual.clips.map((c) => c.name) // ['Walk_Loop', 'Jog_Fwd_Loop', …]
const glb = riggedBodyGlb(body, {
  clips: [{ from: ual, clip: 'Walk_Loop', extras: { license: 'CC0 1.0' } }],
})
```

The skeleton is read as Babylon's `readSkeleton` reads a loaded one, so a
clip retargets the same here as in the [character builder](/character-builder/):
each joint's rest is its node's own transform; a top joint's takes in every
node above it (an armature's turn, and its scale, which every joint below is
put in the model root's units by: Mixamo's centimetres under a 0.01), and so
do its keys. Rotations are sampled with `LINEAR`'s slerp, `STEP` as steps and
`CUBICSPLINE` at its keys' values.

A clip's licence travels with it in its animation's `extras`: UAL's are CC0;
Mixamo's are Adobe's, usable in a project and not to be redistributed on
their own; Meshy's are licensed only with their model.

Pure: no DOM, no Babylon.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/glb-clips/

---

# bvh

Motion capture files (BVH, Biovision Hierarchy) as clips. Decades of mocap
are in this format (the CMU library, Bandai Namco's research set, most
capture suites), and a BVH read here is the same thing as a clip read from a
GLB ([glb-clips](/glb-clips/)): a `GlbClipSource`, its own skeleton and its
clip. So it plays on any body through `bakeClip` or `retargetClip`, which read
which bone is which from the names (CMU's and Mixamo's spellings both work).

- `readBvh(text)` reads one. Rotations are Euler angles in the order each
  joint's CHANNELS line lists them (BVH's rule), turned into quaternions.
  Units are guessed from the skeleton's height (a person stands 1 to 2.5 m;
  centimetres and inches are scaled to metres; anything else is scaled to a
  1.8 m person), or set with `scale`.
- `writeBvh(source, clip)` writes any clip source out (a capture, a UAL clip)
  for Blender, MotionBuilder and other tools. Rest is BVH's: every joint
  unturned, offsets along the world axes, so a skeleton whose joints are
  turned at rest (UAL's, any glTF's) is written as its turns since rest.

Pure, no engine.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/bvh/

---

# clip-store

The clips this browser keeps: motion of your own (a BVH capture, a Mixamo or
Meshy GLB's animations), kept by name as the files they came from, so any
character on the site can play them on its next visit. Captures are like
garments of your own, and this is their wardrobe beside `tosijs-garments`
(IndexedDB `tosijs-clips`).

A kept clip is its FILE's bytes with its kind (`bvh` or `glb`), so it is read
again exactly as it was read the first time ([bvh](/bvh/),
[glb-clips](/glb-clips/)), and a newer reader reads it better.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/clip-store/

---

# rigged-body

**One shape for a character's body, whoever made it.** A rigged body is a
rest mesh on UAL's skeleton with its skin weights: what the
[rig tool](/rig-tool/) makes of any mesh and its markers, and what
[human-rig](/human-rig/) makes of MakeHuman's body and its sliders. Everything
the [character builder](/character-builder/) does with a body (play clips,
stand it on the floor, cut garments, fit hair, dress it) takes a rigged body,
so it works the same on either.

```javascript
import { bodyFromMarkers, buildBody, objTriangles } from 'tosijs-3d'

const body = bodyFromMarkers(objTriangles(text))   // markers guessed
const built = buildBody(scene, 'weasel', body)     // a Babylon skeleton on it
```

THREE PRODUCERS: `bodyFromMarkers` (any mesh and its markers), `humanBodyMaker`
(MakeHuman's sliders), and `loadSkinnedBody` (in [auto-rig](/rig-build/)): a
file already skinned to UAL's skeleton, as Quaternius' characters are or as
you can bind a mesh to it in Blender, taken as it is: its joints, its weights,
no markers. The skeleton to bind to comes with Quaternius'
[Universal Animation Library](https://quaternius.itch.io/universal-animation-library)
and [Universal Base Characters](https://quaternius.itch.io/universal-base-characters)
(CC0, pay what you want; the Blender sources are in the paid tiers): get it
there rather than from the copies this site's demos load.

A rigged body is plain data, Babylon-free:

- **`positions`, `indices`**: the rest mesh, right-handed (as glTF and OBJ
  are): metres, +Y up, facing +Z, its left on +X, in its maker's own frame
  (a file's, standing on y = 0 or near; MakeHuman's is centred on the hips).
  `rig.at('root')` says where its feet are.
- **`rig`**: UAL's 65 joints (`rig.at(name)`), from `fitSkeleton` or MakeHuman's
  joint cubes.
- **`weights`**: four joints and weights per vertex, indexing `rig.joints`.
- **`regions`**: masks, one value per vertex from 0 to 1, where the maker
  knows them: `lips` and `nipples` from MakeHuman. A consumer that wants one
  and finds none does without (or works it out from the shape).
- **`made`**: how it was made, enough to make it again: the markers (and
  where the mesh came from), MakeHuman's slider values, or `skin` (the file's
  own).
- **`uvs`, `colors`, `surfaces`** (a file's, when it has them): its texture
  coordinates, vertex colours (RGBA), and its triangles in runs, one per
  material, each with the file's own material. A consumer draws each surface
  as made or puts its own material on it (the builder's skin).

`buildBody` (in [auto-rig](/rig-build/)) makes it a Babylon skeleton.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/rigged-body/

---

# surroundings

**One budgeted read of what is around a character, and the affordances derived
from it.** Pure — distances and degrees, no Babylon, no rays — so cover can be
tested against a world you type out by hand.

Two halves, and the split is the point:

- **The READ** is a measurement. A ring of bearings × a ladder of heights, each
  holding the distance to the nearest obstruction. It knows nothing about cover,
  climbing or shooting.
- **The QUERIES** are relations between that measurement, a character and a
  threat. `shelterFrom` is not a property of a wall; it depends on your size,
  your stance and where the shooting is coming from.

`MOBILITY-DESIGN.md` argues both, and the second is the one with teeth:

> **Suffixes declare what geometry IS. Affordances describe what a character can
> DO with it, and must be computed.** A `_cover` suffix would be a bug, not a
> shortcut.

## Demo — walk into cover and watch it happen

```js
import { b3d, b3dSkybox, b3dController, sceneDelta, label3d, slider3d } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { makeSurroundings, SurroundingsProbe, shelterFrom, exposure, inShelter, stanceFor, peekSide, muzzleClearance, DEFAULT_HEIGHTS } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { demoSun, orbitCam, patternGround } from 'tosijs-3d/demo-utils'
import { tosi } from 'tosijs'

const demo = tosi({ coverDemo: { range: 1.2, needed: 0.8 } })
const s = demo.coverDemo

let hero = null
let babylon = null
let readout = null
let covered = false

const controller = b3dController({
  mapping: 'biped',
  drive(input, dt) {
    if (!hero) return
    // World-axis walking: this demo is about WHERE you stand, not about driving.
    hero.position.x += input.strafe * dt * 4
    hero.position.z += input.forward * dt * 4
  },
})

const panel = () => [
  label3d({ text: 'Cover' }),
  slider3d({ label: 'reach (m)', value: s.range, min: 0.5, max: 3, step: 0.1, showValue: 'always',
    handleChange: (v) => { s.range = v } }),
  slider3d({ label: 'needed', value: s.needed, min: 0.4, max: 1, step: 0.05, showValue: 'always',
    handleChange: (v) => { s.needed = v } }),
]

const scene = b3d(
  {
    style: 'width:100%;height:100%',
    gamepad: 'left_stick',
    scenePanel: panel,
    sceneCreated(el, BABYLON) {
      babylon = BABYLON
      orbitCam(el, { radius: 26, betaDeg: 35.5, target: [0, 1, 2] })

      const solid = (name, w, h, d, x, y, z) => {
        const m = BABYLON.MeshBuilder.CreateBox(name, { width: w, height: h, depth: d }, el.scene)
        m.position.set(x, y, z)
        const mat = new BABYLON.StandardMaterial(name + '-mat', el.scene)
        mat.diffuseColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.55, 0.52, 0.48)
        m.material = mat
        el.register?.({ meshes: [m] })
        return m
      }

      // A low wall, a pillar, an L-shaped corner, and a railing that is not cover.
      solid('lowwall', 9, 1.1, 0.4, -3, 0.55, 5)
      solid('pillar', 1.2, 2.4, 1.2, 5, 1.2, 4)
      solid('corner-a', 0.4, 2.2, 5, 10, 1.1, 2)
      solid('corner-b', 4, 2.2, 0.4, 8.2, 1.1, 4.6)
      // A railing: top rail only, wide open underneath.
      solid('rail', 6, 0.25, 0.3, -9, 1.05, 5)
      solid('rail-post-a', 0.2, 1.1, 0.2, -11.8, 0.55, 5)
      solid('rail-post-b', 0.2, 1.1, 0.2, -6.2, 0.55, 5)

      const threat = BABYLON.MeshBuilder.CreateSphere('threat', { diameter: 0.9 }, el.scene)
      threat.position.set(0, 1.5, 18)
      const tm = new BABYLON.StandardMaterial('threat-mat', el.scene)
      tm.diffuseColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.9, 0.15, 0.2)
      tm.emissiveColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.5, 0.05, 0.08)
      threat.material = tm

      hero = BABYLON.MeshBuilder.CreateCapsule('hero', { height: 1.8, radius: 0.35 }, el.scene)
      hero.position.set(0, 0.9, -2)
      const hm = new BABYLON.StandardMaterial('hero-mat', el.scene)
      hero.material = hm
      el.register?.({ meshes: [hero] })

      // ONE probe, throttled to 10Hz, reusing its buffers. `SurroundingsProbe`
      // gathers the nearby meshes once per read instead of asking the whole
      // scene 84 times — see "The probe and what it costs", below.
      const surr = makeSurroundings({ bearingCount: 12, heights: DEFAULT_HEIGHTS })
      const probe = new SurroundingsProbe(surr, 10)
      const solidOnly = (m) => m !== hero && m !== threat && m.name !== 'ground' && m.isVisible
      const foot = new BABYLON.Vector3(0, 0, 0)

      el.scene.onBeforeRenderObservable.add(() => {
        const dt = sceneDelta(el.scene)
        const range = Number(s.range)
        // THE FEET, and the feet do not move when he crouches. Deriving them
        // from `position` (a capsule CENTRE, which drops on a crouch) shifts
        // the whole height ladder down with it, so the wall measures taller
        // than it is and the character talks himself out of the cover he is
        // standing behind — while crouching, which lowers it again.
        foot.set(hero.position.x, 0, hero.position.z)
        // `false` means "nothing new to look at" — so the derivation is skipped
        // too, rather than recomputing identical answers sixty times a second.
        if (!probe.update(el.scene, foot, dt, { maxRange: range, filter: solidOnly })) return

        const threatDeg = (Math.atan2(threat.position.x - hero.position.x,
                                      threat.position.z - hero.position.z) * 180) / Math.PI
        const stature = { standing: 1.8, needed: Number(s.needed) }
        const sh = shelterFrom(surr, threatDeg, { maxRange: range })
        // Stance FIRST: how exposed you are depends on what you are doing
        // about it, and a low wall you are crouched behind hides all of you.
        const stance = stanceFor(sh.height, stature)
        const masked = 1 - exposure(sh.height, stature, stance ?? 'standing')
        covered = inShelter(masked, covered)
        const peek = peekSide(surr, threatDeg, { maxRange: range })
        const clear = muzzleClearance(surr, threatDeg, stance === 'crouched' ? 0.9 : 1.45, { maxRange: range })

        hm.diffuseColor = covered
          ? new BABYLON.Color3(0.25, 0.75, 0.35)
          : new BABYLON.Color3(0.9, 0.6, 0.2)
        // Crouch when the cover demands it — derived, like everything else here.
        hero.scaling.y = stance === 'crouched' ? 0.62 : 1
        // Keep the FEET on the floor whatever the stance does.
        hero.position.y = 0.9 * hero.scaling.y

        if (readout) {
          readout.textContent =
            `hidden ${(masked * 100).toFixed(0)}%   cover ${sh.height.toFixed(1)}m   ` +
            `${covered ? 'IN COVER' : 'exposed'}   stance ${stance ?? 'none'}   ` +
            `peek ${peek ?? 'none'}   ${clear > 0 ? `shot BLOCKED (needs ${clear.toFixed(1)}m)` : 'shot clear'}`
        }
      })
    },
  },
  demoSun(),
  b3dSkybox({ timeOfDay: 11 }),
  patternGround({ size: 60 }),
  controller
)

preview.append(scene)
readout = document.createElement('div')
readout.style.cssText = 'position:absolute;bottom:8px;left:8px;right:8px;font:12px monospace;background:#0009;color:#fff;padding:4px 8px;border-radius:4px'
preview.append(readout)
```
```css
.preview { height: 100%; position: relative; }
```

**WASD / left stick** to move. The red sphere is the shooter. The marker turns
green when you are in cover, and the readout says how much of you is hidden,
what stance the cover demands, which side you could lean out of, and whether
your own wall is in the way of your shot.

Things worth doing:

- **Stand behind the long low wall.** You are covered — crouched. Now walk to
  its end and watch cover fall away with nothing pressed and nothing stuck.
- **Stand behind the pillar.** Full cover, and `peek` says `both` — a pillar is
  cover you can shoot past on either side.
- **Walk into the corner.** The wall doing the work is not the one facing the
  shooter, which is why `shelterFrom` searches an arc.
- **Compare the low wall with the railing** (the one on legs). Same height, same
  distance, no cover at all — because a shelter with a gap under it is not a
  shelter.

The rays are cast at 10Hz, not every frame, which is the budget the design
asks for: 12 bearings × 7 heights is 84 casts, and at a walk you move 5cm
between reads.

> **WASD** to move. The marker turns green when the probe says you are in cover
> — walk behind a block and watch it flip, then widen `reach` and watch cover
> start further out.
>
> Cover is DISCOVERED here, not entered: nothing puts you into a cover mode and
> there is no state to leave. The readout is the live answer, which is why it
> can disagree with where you thought you were standing.

## Why a shared read rather than a fan of rays per feature

Also from `MOBILITY-DESIGN.md`:

> when the second consumer appears, **do not give it its own fan of rays.** One
> budgeted environmental read per tick, shared — "what is around me, at what
> heights, how far" — with features asking questions of the result.

Cover is that second consumer. A mantle check is eight casts; cover wants a ring;
"can I get there" wants another; at eight per frame per feature a character
controller eats the frame budget on its own. And a shared read has a second
virtue that matters more than the cost: every feature is then reasoning about
the SAME world. Two private reads disagree at exactly the moment they matter —
the frame you are half behind a wall.

The read is deliberately coarse. Twelve bearings is 30° apart, which sounds
crude until you remember what it is for: a wall you are pressed against occupies
many buckets, and a gap you could be shot through occupies at least one. It is
sampling a room, not tracing a silhouette.

## Heights, not a height

One forward ray at shin height misses a canal bank whose face exists only between
0.25m and 1.25m (undercut below, sloping away above), and the character is then
visibly stuck against a wall the probe says is not there. **Real geometry is not
sampled correctly by a single ray, and the failure is silent**, because a miss
and an absence are the same reading.

So the unit of measurement here is a COLUMN: what is in front of me, at every
height that matters. A low wall and a doorway are the same distance and
completely different affordances, and the only thing that tells them apart is
which heights are blocked.

## Cover is derived, never entered

`shelterFrom` returns how much of you is masked, right now. There is no
`enterCover`, no cover state and nothing to be stuck in — the anti-goal the whole
design is organised around. `inShelter` adds the one bit of state anybody needs,
and it is hysteresis rather than a mode, so the answer does not flicker at its
threshold (the same reason swimming has a band).

## The probe and what it costs

`SurroundingsProbe` is the Babylon half: it casts the rays that fill the read.
`new SurroundingsProbe(surroundings, hz)` and then, each frame,
`probe.update(scene, feet, dt, { maxRange, filter })`, which returns `false` when
no new read was due. It is separate so the pure module stays importable without a
renderer.

One read is **12 bearings × 7 heights = 84 rays**. The probe gathers the nearby
meshes ONCE per read (a bounding-sphere distance test) instead of letting every
ray test every mesh in the scene, so the cost depends on what is **near the
character**, not on how big the level is. Measured in Chrome:

| per read | 11 meshes | 311 | 1011 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `scene.pickWithRay` | 105µs | **2809µs** | — |
| `SurroundingsProbe` | **50µs** | 39µs | **73µs** |

The extra meshes were hundreds of metres away and none was within reach. The
results agree with `pickWithRay` to within 2mm.

The queries on top (`shelterFrom`, `stanceFor`, `exposure`, `inShelter`,
`peekSide`, `muzzleClearance`) together take about **160ns**, roughly 450× less
than the read. The rays are the cost; the thinking is not. At 10Hz, cover
discovery is about **0.7ms of CPU per character per second**, so a tenth of a 60fps
frame covers roughly **140 characters**.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/surroundings/

# auto-rig

**Binding a mesh to a skeleton, with no rig to start from.** Eight markers on
a mesh's front view (chin, groin, wrists, elbows, knees) place UAL's 65-bone
skeleton (`fitSkeleton`), bone heat binds the skin to it (`boneHeat`), and
`buildRig` makes a Babylon skeleton of the result, so `retargetClip` plays
UAL's clips on it and `springNodes` swings a tail.

To do this by hand, use the [rig tool](/rig-tool/): load a GLB or OBJ with
no skeleton (or turn off `use its own skeleton` to ignore the one it has),
drag the markers onto its joints (the skeleton follows each time you let go,
and the skin is bound again when you animate or press done). The markers are
saved in its recipe. This page is the code underneath, for doing
the same in your own page or pipeline.

## Usage

```
import {
  objTriangles, guessMarkers, rigSilhouette, fitSkeleton, meshQuery,
  skinSegments, boneHeat, buildRig, readSkeleton, retargetClip,
} from 'tosijs-3d'

// The mesh as triangles, in its file's own (right-handed) frame,
// facing +Z with its left on +X.
const { positions, indices } = objTriangles(await (await fetch(url)).text())

// Markers: guessed from the outline, or from a rig tool recipe's `binding`.
const markers = recipe?.binding?.markers ??
  guessMarkers(rigSilhouette(positions, indices, 'front'))

const rig = fitSkeleton(markers, meshQuery(positions, indices), {
  tail: recipe?.binding?.tail ?? undefined,
})
const weights = boneHeat(positions, indices, skinSegments(rig))
const built = buildRig(scene, 'weasel', positions, indices, rig, weights)
built.root.parent = stand // move it by a parent of root, never root itself

// ualWalk, ualSkin and ualRoot: a clip, skeleton and __root__ from UAL's GLB.
const walk = retargetClip(ualWalk, readSkeleton(ualSkin, ualRoot),
  readSkeleton(built.skeleton, built.root), { scene })
walk.start(true)
```

For a model file, `loadRigTriangles(scene, urlOrFile, { pick })` reads its
triangles (its own skeleton ignored), and `autoRig(scene, name, tris)` does
the rest in one call (markers guessed unless you pass them), returning the
built rig with its `rig` and `markers`:

```
const body = autoRig(scene, 'body', await loadRigTriangles(scene, url))
body.root.parent = stand
```

A tail, when `fitSkeleton` is given its tip, is the bone chain `tail_01` …
`tail_leaf`: hand `built.node(name)` for each to `springNodes` and it swings.
Binding takes about 0.1 to 0.3 s for 1,000 to 6,000 vertices, so do it once
and keep the result.

## How it is built

AUTO-RIG, THE BABYLON SIDE: a fitted skeleton (`rig-fit`) and its skin
weights (`bone-heat`) become a real Babylon skeleton on a mesh, built the way
the glTF loader builds one, so everything that works on a loaded character
works on it: `readSkeleton` and `retargetClip` play UAL clips on it, and
`springNodes` simulates its tail.

The joints are TransformNodes under one container (`root`), each bone LINKED
to its node, with the mesh under the same container: Babylon then reads each
bone from its node, and the skin and the nodes share a frame.

THE DATA IS RIGHT-HANDED, as OBJ and glTF files are (and as `rig-fit`
assumes: a character facing +Z has its left on +X). Babylon is left-handed,
so the container carries the same mirror glTF's `__root__` does (a half turn
about Y and z scaled by -1). Pass `root` to `readSkeleton` as you would
`__root__`: both measure in the file's own frame. Move the character by a
parent of `root`, not `root` itself.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/rig-build/

# rig markers

**Where the auto-rig's eight markers go, dragged over the mesh.** Mixamo's
auto-rigger asks for eight points on a front view (chin, wrists, elbows,
knees, groin) and works the skeleton out from them. `markerField3d` is that
step: the mesh's front silhouette with the markers on it, dragged where the
joints are. A tail tip, which a front view cannot see, gets a side view
beside it. Symmetry is on by default, so a wrist placed on one side places
the other.

It is an ordinary scene-panel control, so it works on a page, in the scene
and in a headset alike. The [rig tool](/rig-tool/) uses it to bind a
mesh with no skeleton: drag a marker and the mesh is fitted and bound again
when you let go.

## Usage

```javascript
import { markerField3d, fitSkeleton, meshQuery } from 'tosijs-3d'

const field = markerField3d({
  positions, indices,        // the mesh, as triangles (objTriangles reads an OBJ)
  value: markers,            // or leave it out: guessMarkers places them
  tail: { x: 0, y: 0.5, z: -0.9 },   // a tail tip, or leave it out
  handleCommit: (markers, tail) => refit(markers, tail),
})
```

`handleChange` fires as a marker moves; `handleCommit` once, when it is let
go. Fitting and binding take a fraction of a second, so they belong on commit.

## The guess

`guessMarkers(silhouette)` reads the front silhouette:
- **groin:** the crotch, the first filled point going up the centre line;
- **wrists and elbows:** the widest row of the upper body (the arms of a
  T-pose);
- **knees:** the middle of each leg, a little over halfway from the floor to
  the crotch;
- **chin:** the narrowest row between the arms and the top of the head (the
  neck).

It is a starting point to drag from, not a fit. A tail that hangs between
the legs hides the crotch, and an A-pose has no widest row of arms; both
fall back to proportions.

## Coordinates

Markers are in the mesh's own units and frame, as `fitSkeleton` takes them:
the character faces +Z with its left on +X, so in the front view its left is
on your right. The side view has +Z (the front) on the right.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/rig-markers/

# spring bones

**Hair, tails and cloaks that follow the body.** A chain of bones nobody
animates — a ponytail, a tail, a strand of a cape — swings, trails and
settles on its own, after the body's animation has posed it each frame. The
body is animated; the hair is simulated.

## Demo

```js
import { b3d, b3dLight, assetUrl, select3d, slider3d, springBones, boneHeat, sceneDelta } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { tosi } from 'tosijs'

const { hair } = tosi({ hair: { clip: 'Jog_Fwd_Loop', stiffness: 0.1, damping: 0.6 } })
const clips = ['Idle_Loop', 'Walk_Loop', 'Jog_Fwd_Loop', 'Sprint_Loop', 'Dance_Loop']
const speeds = { Idle_Loop: 0, Walk_Loop: 1.4, Jog_Fwd_Loop: 3, Sprint_Loop: 5.5, Dance_Loop: 0 }

preview.append(
  b3d(
    {
      clearColor: '#2a3340',
      scenePanelOpen: true,
      panelTitle: 'Ponytail',
      scenePanel: () => [
        select3d({ label: 'clip', value: hair.clip, options: clips }),
        slider3d({ label: 'stiffness', value: hair.stiffness, min: 0, max: 1, step: 0.01 }),
        slider3d({ label: 'damping', value: hair.damping, min: 0, max: 0.99, step: 0.01 }),
      ],
      async sceneCreated(el, BABYLON) {
        const scene = el.scene
        const cam = new BABYLON.ArcRotateCamera('c', Math.PI / 3, 1.3, 3.2, new BABYLON.Vector3(0, 1, 0), scene)
        cam.attachControl(el.querySelector('canvas'), true)
        el.setActiveCamera(cam)
        BABYLON.MeshBuilder.CreateGround('g', { width: 12, height: 12 }, scene)

        const ual = await BABYLON.LoadAssetContainerAsync(assetUrl('quaternius/UAL1_core.glb', 3), scene)
        ual.addAllToScene()
        for (const g of ual.animationGroups) g.stop()
        const root = ual.meshes.find((m) => m.name === '__root__')
        const node = (n) => ual.transformNodes.find((t) => t.name === n)
        const head = node('Head')

        // Where the ponytail hangs, measured off the body in its rest pose:
        // forward is from the heel to the toes, up the back of the skull.
        root.computeWorldMatrix(true)
        for (const t of ual.transformNodes) t.computeWorldMatrix(true)
        const at = (n) => node(n).getAbsolutePosition().clone()
        const fwd = at('ball_leaf_l').subtract(at('foot_l')).multiplyByFloats(1, 0, 1).normalize()
        const up = new BABYLON.Vector3(0, 1, 0)
        const start = at('Head').add(up.scale(0.13)).subtract(fwd.scale(0.1))
        const dir = fwd.scale(-0.45).add(up.scale(-0.9)).normalize()
        const points = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].map((i) => start.add(dir.scale(0.075 * i)))

        const pony = springBones(scene, head, points, {
          colliders: [
            { node: head, radius: 0.12, offset: up.scale(0.09) },
            { node: node('spine_03'), radius: 0.17 },
            { node: node('clavicle_l'), radius: 0.09 },
            { node: node('clavicle_r'), radius: 0.09 },
          ],
          params: { stiffness: hair.stiffness.value, damping: hair.damping.value },
        })
        hair.stiffness.observe(() => (pony.params.stiffness = hair.stiffness.value))
        hair.damping.observe(() => (pony.params.damping = hair.damping.value))

        // A tube around the chain, skinned to it by bone heat.
        const tube = pony.skinTube({ radius: 0.035, tipRadius: 0.012, sides: 8, boneHeat })
        const mat = new BABYLON.StandardMaterial('hair', scene)
        mat.diffuseColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.45, 0.25, 0.1)
        mat.backFaceCulling = false
        tube.material = mat

        // Run round a circle at the clip's own speed, so the hair trails.
        // (A node above glTF's root, whose mirror and turn stay as loaded.)
        const runner = new BABYLON.TransformNode('runner', scene)
        root.parent = runner
        const yaw0 = Math.atan2(fwd.x, fwd.z)
        // The camera follows the runner, at head height.
        const look = new BABYLON.TransformNode('look', scene)
        look.parent = runner
        look.position.y = 1.35
        cam.setTarget(look)
        let angle = 0
        const radius = 2.2
        scene.onBeforeAnimationsObservable.add(() => {
          angle += ((speeds[hair.clip.value] ?? 0) * sceneDelta(scene)) / radius
          runner.position.set(Math.cos(angle) * radius, 0, Math.sin(angle) * radius)
          runner.rotation.y = Math.atan2(-Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle)) - yaw0
        })
        let playing = null
        const play = (name) => {
          playing?.stop()
          playing = ual.animationGroups.find((g) => g.name === name)
          playing?.start(true)
        }
        play(hair.clip.value)
        hair.clip.observe(() => play(hair.clip.value))
      },
    },
    b3dLight({ intensity: 0.9 })
  )
)
```

A UAL mannequin with a ponytail it was not made with: six bones hung from
the head, a tube skinned to them by bone heat, and the chain simulated.
Change the clip, or the stiffness and damping, in the panel.

## Use

`springBones(scene, anchor, points, options)` hangs a chain from `anchor` (any
TransformNode: a glTF bone's node, or a mesh) through `points` (world, in the
rest pose), makes a TransformNode per joint under the anchor, and simulates
them every frame after animations run. Options:

| option | |
| --- | --- |
| `params` | `stiffness` (0 hangs free, 1 holds its rest shape), `damping` (velocity lost per second), `gravity`, `radius` |
| `colliders` | spheres the chain stays out of: `{ node, radius, offset? }` |

It returns `{ nodes, params, skinTube(options), reset(), dispose() }`.
`nodes` are the chain's joints, to parent your own meshes to; `skinTube`
builds a tube skinned to them (pass `boneHeat` to weight it). Call `reset()`
after a teleport. The pure model is `spring-chain`: Verlet at a fixed 120 Hz
step, lengths solved from the root with Müller's follow-the-leader damping
(otherwise the tip cracks like a whip for seconds).

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/spring-chain-babylon/

# b3d-aircraft

Fly-by-wire VTOL controller — a forgiving "drone that becomes a plane" rather
than a simulation. The stick commands an ATTITUDE (bank + pitch); the craft eases
toward it and self-levels when you let go, banking swings the heading (a
coordinated turn), and the velocity simply chases where the nose points. The
model is pure and unit-tested in [fly-by-wire](/fly-by-wire/).

Mesh can come from a `url` (own GLB) or from a `b3d-library` via `library` + `meshName`.
The full flight model is explained below the demo.

## Demo

```js
import { b3d, b3dAircraft, b3dRadar, b3dRadarBlip, b3dHud, b3dClouds, b3dFog, b3dLibrary, b3dDestroyable, b3dDeath, b3dLight, b3dSun, b3dSkybox, b3dGround, b3dWeatherCell, gameController, inputFocus, sceneDelta, slider3d } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { elements } from 'tosijs'
const { div } = elements

const RADAR_RANGE = 250 // nominal radar range (m); a profile-1 blip detects within it
const MAX_ALT = 300     // the aircraft's ceiling (its `ceiling`, default 300)

// A FACTORY — so a respawn is a genuinely new aircraft (with its radar), not a reset. The sim
// really emits a death and a spawn, which is the stream a narrative driver reads (see b3d-death).
// The HUD shows in BOTH views: in-scene on the canopy in cockpit, flat overlay in chase
// (minus the artificial horizon, which only tells the truth from inside the aircraft).
const plane = () => b3dAircraft(
  { library: 'vehicles', meshName: 'scout', player: true, y: 0, vtolSpeed: 6, maxSpeed: 55 },
  b3dRadar({ range: RADAR_RANGE, coneDeg: 90, lockTime: 1.2, maxLocks: 2 }),
)
// A respawned aircraft is appended INSIDE the focus manager; it announces itself when ready
// (adoptIfVacant) and the manager takes it because it's driving nobody.
const focus = inputFocus(gameController(), plane())

// A target = a destroyable cube that is ALSO a radar-blip (nested, so the blip follows it).
// Faction picks the colour + whether the radar locks it: HOSTILE locks, NEUTRAL only shows.
function target({ faction, ...pos }) {
  const color = faction === 'hostile' ? '#d05050' : '#c7ad55'
  return b3dDestroyable(
    { meshName: 'drone', size: 2.4, color, capacity: 6, ...pos,
      explode: 'on', explodeForce: 8,
      deathBlast: 'on', blastDamage: 10, blastFullRadius: 2, blastRadius: 6 },
    b3dRadarBlip({ faction, profile: 1 }),
  )
}
function scatter(aerial) {
  const d = RADAR_RANGE * (0.5 + Math.random()) // 0.5x..1.5x range
  const az = (Math.random() - 0.5) * (170 * Math.PI / 180) // +/-85 deg around the nose (+Z)
  return target({
    faction: Math.random() < 0.65 ? 'hostile' : 'neutral',
    x: Math.sin(az) * d,
    z: Math.cos(az) * d,
    y: aerial ? MAX_ALT * (0.1 + Math.random() * 1.15) : 1.0 + Math.random() * 1.2,
  })
}
const air = Array.from({ length: 12 }, () => scatter(true))
const ground = Array.from({ length: 8 }, () => scatter(false))
const targets = [...air, ...ground]

const kills = div({ class: 'kills' }, `Targets down: 0 / ${targets.length}`)
// WEATHER, to fly in: a storm cell over the whole arena (storminess shakes
// the airframe) and the scene's wind (it carries you; blowing east, across
// your starting heading, so you crab). Both on the settings panel.
const storm = b3dWeatherCell({ x: 0, z: 0, radius: 3000, storminess: 0 })
const turb = div({ class: 'turb' }, 'turbulence 0.00')
let down = 0

const scene = b3d(
  {
    gamepad: true,
    // EXPERIMENT (chasePitchFollow): how much of the nose's pitch the chase camera
    // inherits. 0 = the level pivot (the plane pitches within a steady frame);
    // 1 = as if the camera were bolted to the airframe, so a climb aims the view
    // up. It's a slider because the right answer is a matter of taste and you can
    // only judge it while flying — in the headset as much as flat.
    windBearingDeg: 90,
    scenePanel: (el) => [
      slider3d({ label: 'wind (m/s)', min: 0, max: 30, step: 1, value: 0,
        handleChange(v) { el.windSpeed = v } }),
      slider3d({ label: 'storminess', min: 0, max: 1, step: 0.05, value: 0,
        handleChange(v) { storm.storminess = v } }),
      slider3d({ label: 'chase pitch follow', min: 0, max: 1, step: 0.05, value: 0,
        handleChange(v) {
          el.querySelectorAll('tosi-b3d-aircraft').forEach((a) => { a.chasePitchFollow = v })
        } }),
      slider3d({ label: 'follow lag', min: 0.5, max: 12, step: 0.5, value: 3,
        handleChange(v) {
          el.querySelectorAll('tosi-b3d-aircraft').forEach((a) => { a.chasePitchLag = v })
        } }),
    ],
    sceneCreated(el) {
      el.addEventListener('destroyed', () => {
        down += 1
        kills.textContent = `Targets down: ${down} / ${targets.length}`
      })
      // Drift the AIR targets so they move on radar but stay hittable.
      let t = 0
      el.scene.onBeforeRenderObservable.add(() => {
        t += sceneDelta(el.scene)
        const a = el.querySelector('tosi-b3d-aircraft')
        if (a) turb.textContent = `turbulence ${(a.turbulenceLevel ?? 0).toFixed(2)}`
        air.forEach((d, i) => {
          if (d.dead) return
          d.x += Math.sin(t * 0.3 + i) * 0.02
          d.y += Math.sin(t * 0.6 + i * 2) * 0.01
        })
      })
    },
  },
  b3dLight({ y: 1, intensity: 0.45 }),
  b3dSun({ x: -0.6, y: -1, z: -0.4, intensity: 0.9, shadowTextureSize: 2048, shadowMaxZ: 300, activeDistance: 150, updateIntervalMs: 50 }),
  b3dSkybox({ timeOfDay: 10 }),
  b3dFog({ start: 200, end: 1200, color: '#cfe0f2' }),
  b3dGround({ meshName: 'ground_nocast', width: 900, height: 900, color: '#7d9b6e' }),
  b3dLibrary({ url: '/test-3.glb', type: 'vehicles' }),
  // Fly UP into the cloud layer — the whiteout is fog (stereo-safe) and reads insideCloud.
  b3dClouds({ model: '/cloud.glb', altitude: 120, thickness: 40, size: 60, coverage: 0.45, castShadows: true, seed: 4 }),
  b3dHud({}),
  // A nav waypoint far ahead: a positional blip (no mesh), always detectable (profile -1).
  b3dRadarBlip({ faction: 'waypoint', profile: -1, x: 0, y: 25, z: 300 }),
  storm,
  ...targets,
  // DEATH NEEDS AN EXIT: fly into the ground (or get caught in a blast) and it burns, releases
  // input, orbits the wreck, then floats a Respawn panel — which appends a fresh aircraft.
  b3dDeath({ title: 'DOWN', spectate: 'chase', respawn() { focus.appendChild(plane()) } }),
  focus,
)
preview.append(scene, kills, turb)
```

tosi-b3d { flex: 1; min-height: 0; width: 100%; }
.turb {
  padding: 6px 12px; border-radius: 4px;
  background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.55); color: #9fdcf0; font: 14px monospace;
}
