# Pseudo Random Numbers

**Randomness you can replay.** Everything procedural here (a galaxy, a
planet's craters, where the rocks go, who spawns) is drawn from a generator
started from a number, the SEED. Same seed, same numbers, in every browser,
so the same seed is the same world: you can share it, test it, and come back
to it.

Nothing here uses `Math.random()`. It cannot be seeded, so it can never give
you the same world twice, and it is not very random: the standard does not
say which algorithm it is, so its quality is whatever the browser shipped.
That has been bad. V8's before 2015 (MWC1616) had cycles short enough, and
patterns plain enough, to see in a picture of its output; engines are better
now, but "better now, in some browsers" is not something to build on.

We implement two generators, each for a job:

- **`PRNG`** (on **xoshiro128\*\***) for the general case: a stream of good
  numbers with convenience methods (ranges, a bell curve, weighted picks).
- **`CheapPRNG`** (on **mulberry32**) for derived data: one tiny generator
  per object, built, drawn from a few times, and dropped, millions of times
  over (a star's name and its details).

## Demo

```js
import { PRNG } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { elements } from 'tosijs'
const { div, p, button, pre } = elements

let output = ''
const prng = new PRNG(42)

output += 'Seed: 42\n\n'
output += 'value():        ' + prng.value().toFixed(6) + '\n'
output += 'range(1, 100):  ' + prng.range(1, 100) + '\n'
output += 'realRange(0,1): ' + prng.realRange(0, 1).toFixed(6) + '\n'
output += 'gaussrandom():  ' + prng.gaussrandom().toFixed(6) + '\n'
output += 'probability(0.5): ' + prng.probability(0.5) + '\n'
output += 'pick([a,b,c]):  ' + prng.pick(['a', 'b', 'c']) + '\n'
output += 'pick weighted:  ' + prng.pick(['rare', 'common'], [1, 99]) + '\n\n'

output += 'Deterministic check (new PRNG(42)):\n'
const prng2 = new PRNG(42)
output += 'value():        ' + prng2.value().toFixed(6) + ' (same as above)\n'

preview.append(pre(output))
```

## Why these two

What we need from a generator, in order: the **same sequence everywhere**
(pure 32-bit integer arithmetic, `Math.imul` and shifts, so no engine's
floating point can change it), **seeded by one number**, then **cheap to
start**, and good enough statistically for games. Cryptographic strength is
not on the list: nothing here is a secret.

Measured in Bun, building one and drawing 8 numbers:

| Generator | State | Build + 8 draws | One draw |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mersenne Twister (MT19937) | 624 words | 13 µs | 0.02 µs |
| xoshiro128\*\* (`PRNG`) | 4 words | 0.09 µs | 0.01 µs |
| mulberry32 (`CheapPRNG`) | 1 word | 0.03 µs | 0.008 µs |

**xoshiro128\*\*** (Blackman and Vigna) is behind `PRNG`, not the Mersenne
Twister this page is named after: MT has a huge state that it fills before its
first draw, so merely starting one costs about 13 µs, and a star system starts one per planet while scoring candidate
systems starts thousands. xoshiro128\*\* starts about 150× faster, has a period
of 2¹²⁸, and passes the BigCrush and PractRand test batteries, which MT does
not (it fails the linear-complexity tests). Its one integer seed is spread
over its four words by splitmix32, which also keeps it out of the all-zero
state it could never leave.

**mulberry32** is smaller still: one 32-bit word, a few multiplies a draw. It
is weaker (a period of 2³², and each seed is one short stream), and that does
not matter for what it does: a handful of draws per star, each a pure
function of the star's seed. It is about 3× cheaper than xoshiro to start,
which counts at galaxy scale, and more to the point its output IS the galaxy:
star names and spectral details are drawn from it, so changing its engine
would rename every star. It stays.

**The Mersenne Twister** is still exported (`MersenneTwister`), for sequences
that must match older `PRNG` output, which was built on it. Nothing here uses it.

A few places hash rather than generate: noise lattices (`noise-volume`,
`climate-noise`) fill bytes with xorshift32, and `latticeHash` turns a grid
point into a number directly. A hash answers "what is the number AT this
place" with no sequence to step through, which is what a texture or an
infinite grid needs.

## API

### `Xoshiro128`, `MersenneTwister`

The bare engines, for when you want numbers and nothing else.

| Method | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `constructor(seed)` | | Create with a numeric seed (required: pass `Date.now()` for a different sequence each run) |
| `random()` | `number` | Random float in [0, 1) |
| `int32()` | `number` | Random 32-bit unsigned integer |

### `PRNG`

| Method | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `constructor(seed)` | | Create with numeric seed |
| `value()` | `number` | Random float in [0, 1) |
| `range(min, max)` | `number` | Random integer in [min, max] |
| `realRange(min, max, skew?)` | `number` | Random float in [min, max) with optional skew function |
| `gaussrandom(dev?)` | `number` | Gaussian random with given standard deviation (default 1) |
| `probability(p)` | `boolean` | Returns true with probability p |
| `pick(array, weights?)` | `T` | Weighted random selection from array |


### `CheapPRNG`

The same surface as `PRNG` less `gaussrandom` (`value`, `range`,
`realRange`, `probability`, `pick`), on mulberry32. `RandomLike` is the part
both share, for a function that takes either.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/mersenne-twister/

# perlin-noise

**Seeded 3D Perlin noise.** The same seed always gives the same field, which
is what terrain, clouds and everything else procedural here is built on.

```javascript
import { PerlinNoise } from 'tosijs-3d/perlin-noise'

const noise = new PerlinNoise(1234) // always pass a seed
noise.noise3D(x, y, z) // about -1..1, smooth
noise.noise2D(x, y)
noise.fractal(x, y, z, 6, 0.5, 2) // octaves, persistence, lacunarity
```

Leave the seed out and you get a different field every time, which is rarely
what you want. Noise is 0 at every whole-number coordinate, so scale your
inputs (`x * 0.01`) and do not sample on the integer grid.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/perlin-noise/

---

# Noise texture

Shader noise **read instead of computed**. Arithmetic noise in a fragment
shader is the expensive way to get noise: eight hashed corners a sample, every
pixel, every frame, and a cloud pixel takes 54 samples. Reading a texture
replaces that with one fetch, and a mip-mapped texture also fades to its
average in the distance where computed noise shimmers. The ground shader
([[biome-plugin]]), planet surfaces and planet clouds use it.

## Noise volume

`noiseVolume` is a block of 3D gradient noise that **tiles in every
direction**, as bytes. It is pure (no engine, seeded), so the same seed is the
same ground everywhere.

```javascript
import { noiseVolume } from 'tosijs-3d'
const bytes = noiseVolume(64, 16) // 64 texels a side, repeating every 16 cells
```

A value is `0.5 + 0.5 * gain * n`, where `n` is the noise in about -0.9 to 0.9.
The average is 0.5, so a shader reads `texel * 2 - 1`.

## Value noise in GLSL

For value noise the lattice is a 3D texture with one random byte a point
(`latticeVolume`); the shader eases the fraction itself and the linear filter
does the eight-corner blend, so it is the same noise from one read. Neighbouring
cells always agree about a shared corner, which an arithmetic hash on a headset
GPU does not guarantee.

`NOISE_TEXTURE_GLSL` defines `b3dVn(p)` (0…1, like `b3dGgNoise`) and
`b3dVnFbm(p)` (like `b3dGgFbm`). With `B3D_NOISETEX` undefined (no 3D
textures: WebGL 1) they are the arithmetic ones, so it must come after
`GAS_GIANT_GLSL`.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/noise-texture/

# Design notes

Remarks of Tonio Loewald's that decided how something works. The reference
pages say what is true now and why; this page keeps the original words, with
a line on what each one settled and a link to the page it shaped.

## Interfaces

- _"We need popups to be popups and not constrained by the thing that pops
  them. Otherwise the user experience is terrible."_ A popup is its own
  surface in front of its opener, never cropped inside it
  ([popup-surface](/popup-surface/)).
- _"Parenting in 3d is merely positional and not cropping."_ So a popup can
  be parented to its opener in a scene, where a DOM portal could not
  ([popup-surface](/popup-surface/)).
- _"We shouldn't make special size allowances for XR UI targets, we should
  scale XR so that pointer or touch targets make sense, since XR users also
  need to be able to read stuff."_ A headset scales the panel, not the
  targets ([icon-grid](/icon-grid/)).
- _"Panel dragging seems simple enough. Drag it on the surface of a sphere
  around its rig anchor."_ And for its limits: _"It could follow you and
  rubber band back."_ ([frame-panel](/frame-panel/)).
- _"Use the same approach for all our panels as it will also allow
  translucent themes."_ Popups are drawn like every other panel, blended but
  still ordered by depth ([frame-panel](/frame-panel/)).
- _"Simple things like XYZ coords take up huge amounts of space."_ A
  coordinate takes one row ([vector-field](/vector-field/)).
- _"The footprint would work MUCH better as a radial editor. A hexagon would
  just be a hexagon."_ ([footprint-field](/footprint-field/)).
- _"Select move rotate scale, where scale turns off move and rotate, and move
  and rotate turn off scale but can coexist and select is independent."_ The
  tool-palette rule: the grid owns layout, the consumer owns meaning
  ([icon-grid](/icon-grid/)).
- _"The intensity slider goes from 0 to 1000 with very little wiggle-room in
  0-1."_ The case for log sliders ([widgets3d](/widgets3d/)).
- _"The theme editor seems to change the global theme and infects other
  demos."_ Said from a headset; the editor restores the palette when you
  leave ([w3d-theme](/w3d-theme/)).
- _"Presumably we need to be able to configure the light's basic properties
  (like its basic color, intensity, whether it casts shadows, the type of
  light, and so on, or we've only done half the job."_ The lamp editor edits
  the whole lamp ([b3d-lamp](/b3d-lamp/)).

## Curves and light

- _"Let's assume we don't allow mapping outside of `[0,1]` and instead scale
  the terrain block to avoid playing badly with carving."_ A curve's range is
  closed; amplitude belongs to the block ([curve-field](/curve-field/)).
- _"The attack and decay should be shared by the various curves or it just
  becomes nutty."_ A light program's curves share one pair of markers
  ([curve-program](/curve-program/)).
- _"If one curve covers attack - sustain - decay and you simply move the
  point where attack becomes sustain and sustain becomes decay then the only
  real discontinuities will occur mid-loop shut off or shut off while
  spinning up."_ One curve per channel, two markers
  ([light-modulation](/light-modulation/)).
- _"You might not want flicker to compose. The classic fluorescent light
  flickers to life. And if you want the lamp to flicker as it dies, make it
  flicker as it dies."_ Flicker does not compose across regions; draw the tail
  you want ([light-modulation](/light-modulation/)).
- _"The light that looks red doesn't seem to produce red light."_ So the
  dying fluorescent holds an ember ([b3d-lamp](/b3d-lamp/)).
- _"Can we do gels on point lights … if I wanted to make a lamp shaped like
  it's behind a grill like an old lantern?"_ Model the grill; a point light
  takes no gel ([b3d-lamp](/b3d-lamp/)).

## Sky, weather and worlds

- _"What we have is not worthy of everything else we've got. It looks like a
  child's cartoon next to everything else."_ On seeing the blob clouds from
  both sides in a rocket. That is why the cloud deck exists
  ([b3d-cloud-deck](/b3d-cloud-deck/)).
- _"If we use a bunch of quads we can use the vertex channels to drive
  localized weather effects later. Or have clouds that cluster near mountains
  say."_ The deck is a grid, and orographic cloud uses its channels
  ([b3d-cloud-deck](/b3d-cloud-deck/)).
- _"Having a single decal (even if it has less coverage) that is driven by
  the cloud shader logic seems like a performance and appearance win."_ The
  cloud shadow reads the deck's own field ([b3d-cloud-deck](/b3d-cloud-deck/)).
- _"Vectors sum fine don't they?"_ Wind is a vector inside and degrees at the
  edge ([wind](/wind/)).
- _"Given a starfield background is a very specific kind of image I imagine
  we could encode something very efficient in say a 512 or 1024 map by
  treating the values as data."_ The origin of the encoded sky
  ([starfield-codec](/starfield-codec/)).
- _"Almost any star system with planets … is going to have a ball of rock
  someone can plant a flag on."_ So a rocky planet alone does not make a star
  interesting ([b3d-galaxy](/b3d-galaxy/)).
- _"If you change the rules for star system generation expecting things not
  to change is bizarre."_ A star's address may move when the rules change
  ([b3d-galaxy](/b3d-galaxy/)).

## Crowds and animation

- _"I don't really care if my 200 soldiers are a little jerky."_ Soldiers
  bake at a low rate, without interpolation
  ([vertex-animation](/vertex-animation/)).
- _"We have a fallback to handle things like flocks of birds flying around in
  the background, or swarms of insects etc. It's very nice to have, and we
  should definitely keep the infrastructure we built."_
  ([vertex-animation](/vertex-animation/)).
- _"The winged creature is probably more like a dragon and has a slow
  majestic flap."_ A bake's rate follows motion on screen, not the clip's
  speed ([b3d-crowd](/b3d-crowd/)).
- _"A dragon unit will likely be ONE figure or maybe three."_ Unit size
  decides between a crowd and skinned rigs ([b3d-crowd](/b3d-crowd/)).
- _"I think we'd leave the rules for switching to skinned models to the
  consumer since it will be more likely decided on specifics."_ When a crowd
  figure becomes a rig is the consumer's policy ([b3d-crowd](/b3d-crowd/)).
- _"I imagine things like collision detection and so on could vastly
  outweigh the animation costs."_ The crowd bench measures rendering only
  ([b3d-crowd](/b3d-crowd/)).
- _"In the original game the figures were walking on a virtual game board
  and basically offset within a square, so basically collision detection was
  just were you trying to enter an occupied square."_ Grid occupancy, from the
  Amiga original.

## Characters and weapons

- _"When you swim to the water's edge, you just pop instantly to the surface
  onto the land."_ That led to mantling as a general verb rather than a swim
  exit ([b3d-biped](/b3d-biped/)).
- _"The same sort of correction could handle the medium boundary issue."_ The
  wall correction and the waterline band are one camera model
  ([b3d-biped](/b3d-biped/)).
- _"Technically not hard, but having it not look terrible is a whole other
  thing."_ On layered animation, the constraint the bone mask is built around
  ([animation-layers](/animation-layers/)).
- _"I collided with wreckage high up … the wrecked plane hanging in mid-air
  (it should really tumble to the ground)."_ Said from a headset; wreckage
  falls ([b3d-death](/b3d-death/)).
- _"Fine tuning the gun's position by typing is horrible :)"_ So Weapon Fit
  uses a drag gizmo ([weapon-fit](/weapon-fit/)).
- _"A real gun would have fingers wrapped and spread around it. When I model
  the actual weapons — or adapt others' models — I should make the grips a
  little narrower so they don't look weird."_
  ([b3d-launcher](/b3d-launcher/)).

## Content

- _"Making all this cheaply discoverable would facilitate piracy and it's not
  my content."_ A library's catalogue lives inside its GLB; the CDN has no
  index ([glb-manifest](/glb-manifest/)).

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/design-notes/

# Acknowledgements

tosijs-3d stands on other people's work: models, maps, measurements, icons,
libraries and ideas. Most of it was given away with no conditions at all
(CC0, public domain), and is credited here anyway, because someone made it.

## Corrections and takedowns

If something here is yours and the credit is wrong or missing, or you want it
taken down, post in the feedback channel on the
[tosijs Discord](https://discord.gg/ramJ9rgky5) and say what it is and where
it appears. We will fix the credit, or remove the
content from this site and from the asset CDN (`cdn.tosijs.net`), promptly and
without argument.

Every file the CDN serves carries its credit and licence in its own HTTP
headers, so a file found on its own still says where it came from.

  icons. MIT.
- **[Lucide](https://lucide.dev)** (Lucide Contributors): the standing figure
  and the backpack on the inventory. ISC.

## Software

- **[Babylon.js](https://www.babylonjs.com)**: the engine everything here
  draws with. Apache 2.0.
- **[Jolt Physics](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics.js)** (Jorrit Rouwe):
  physics. MIT.
- **[fflate](https://101arrowz.github.io/fflate)** (Arjun Barrett): the
  compression inside the PNG encoder. MIT.
- **[Blender](https://www.blender.org)** (Blender Foundation): converts the
  model packs for the CDN. GPL; nothing of Blender ships.

## Ideas

- Binding a mesh to its skeleton by bone heat: Ilya Baran and Jovan Popović,
  [Automatic Rigging and Animation of 3D Characters](https://people.csail.mit.edu/ibaran/papers/2007-SIGGRAPH-Pinocchio.pdf)
  (SIGGRAPH 2007).
- Hair and tails that do not stretch: Matthias Müller et al., follow-the-leader
  correction, in
  [Fast Simulation of Inextensible Hair and Fur](https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/publications/FTLHairFur.pdf)
  (2012).
- Fitting clothes to any body: MakeHuman's proxy binding, three body vertices
  and an offset per garment vertex.

Source: https://3d.tosijs.net/acknowledgements/
